Issued at 250 AM MDT Sat Oct 10 2026

Being a member of Gen X, I was the first generation to watch Sesame 
Street when I was a wee lad many eons ago. And at the end, right 
before the closing credits, they always said the episode was 
sponsored by two letters. Well, this Area Forecast Discussion is 
sponsored by the letters T and U. T stands for transition, as we 
move from the warm and dry pattern into a cooler and wetter one. And 
U is for uncertainty, as are still a fair amount of questions with 
the forecast, especially in regards to the snowfall potential at the 
lower elevations and details of the forecast toward the middle and 
end of next week.

The T for transition will be today. We had a few showers yesterday, 
and radar shows more showers, generally of the light variety moving 
from Idaho and Utah with the first hits of moisture. The players in 
the forecast remain the same, a cold front dropping in from Montana, 
an upper level low and associated trough dropping in from the 
Pacific Northwest and Tropical Storm Rachel. The cold front should 
remain largely north of the border today, so we will likely have one 
more warm day today, maybe the warmest for the rest of the calendar 
year. Some warmer spots will likely see another high in the 90s. We 
will also have continued gusty wind in the favored southwest flow 
locations from Rock Springs to southern Johnson County.  As for 
showers, moisture from Rachel will increase through the day, drawn 
northward by the trough. The best chance of showers and storms will 
be largely West of the Divide today as downsloping flow should limit 
shower East of the Divide through the daylight hours. There will 
still be some, but not as numerous as West of the Divide. And there 
will likely be some thunderstorms today, as there is decent CAPE for 
October, up to 300 J/Kg with lifted indices down to minus 2. 
Coverage of showers looks to increase tonight as deeper moisture 
moves northward and some jet energy moves into the area, increasing 
upper level divergence.

The wettest day still looks to be Sunday, as the deepest moisture 
from Rachel moves across the area. Reasoning today is fairly similar 
to yesterday. There will be locally heavy rain. Precipitable water 
values could be as high as 0.75 inches, which is close to 200 
percent of the mean and could be a daily record for Sunday. The jet 
will also be nearby, keeping upper level divergence around. Again, 
the placement of the heaviest precipitation will be across western 
Wyoming, with decreasing chances and amounts further to the east. I 
will discuss potential amounts later in the discussion. I did give 
some consideration to flood watches, but decided against them for 
now for the following reasons. One, it has been very dry over the 
past couple of weeks, so there is decent amount of room in the soil 
to soak up some of the rain. Two, the cold front will be further 
south today, and instability will be limited. So, precipitation 
looks more stratiform than convective, which should limit 
precipitation rates somewhat. Three, some of the highest elevations 
may be seeing snow at this point, limiting runoff. I will discuss 
snowfall mounts later in the discussion as well. And four, most 
deterministic models and a majority of the ensemble members show the 
best QPF remaining west of Wyoming. The area I would be most 
concerned about would be the western slopes of the Wind River Range 
with the upslope flow, the Tetons as well as Yellowstone Park. We 
still have time to decide though as the heaviest rain wouldn't be 
until Sunday, with most guidance zeroing in between noon and 
late Sunday night, with some decrease after that as the deepest
moisture from Rachel moves away to the north and east.

By Monday, the dominant feature will be the Upper Level which by 
this point will begin to turn eastward toward the Rockies. Most 
guidance shows lighter precipitation Monday afternoon, and most
confined to areas West of the Divide by that time, with only 
lighter amounts East, Most will also be confined to southern 
Wyoming, with northern Wyoming largely dry. 

We will now discuss precipitation amounts, I will reference from 
Saturday night through Monday, when the most rain is expected to 
fall. The vast majority of the area has at least a 1 in 2 chance of 
a quarter of an inch or precipitation or more, with the smallest 
chance south and east of a Rock Springs to Casper line. Chances of 
an inch or more (greater than 1 in 4 chance) are largely confined 
the northwestern Wyoming as well as the Bighorns where there will be 
an upslope component. The areas with a greater than 2 inches of 
precipitation, which is where the best chance of excessive rainfall 
would be is in western Yellowstone Park, the Tetons and the Wind
